text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Thursday. Prepared for Reuters by the Co-operation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:

- Returning from holiday in Britain, Prime minister Andris Shkele admitted that the government may have to resign after losing several ministers in a corruption scandal and amid a row over a deal between energy supplier Latvenergo and Banka Baltiya, which resulted in a loss of three million lats to the state. Major parties agree with Shkele and are already talking about a new government.

- The foreign ministry said the European Commission used outdated figures when preparing its conclusions on Latvia's readiness to start EU talks. Officials said Latvia would do its best to meet the EU criteria by December, when EU leaders make the final decision on whom to invite to talks.

- The prosecutor's office allowed journalists to look through the file on the investigation of whether Shkele has broken anti-corruption laws, some of which is secret and not for publication. Many journalists declined the offer as a restriction on democracy.

- Diena continues to investigate the scandalous deal between collapsed Banka Baltija and Latvenergo. Latvenergo said that its debt to the bankrupt bank had been transferred to another bank. The liquidator of Banka Baltija said that ceding the debt to a Liechtenstein company was the best way to get the money back.
- Prosecutors investigating whether ministers are corrupt deny being influenced by outside pressure.
- Experts concluded that the voices of the blackmailer Viktor, who threatened bomb attacks by the internet, and Oleg N, arrested last Friday, are identical.

- A conference devoted to the prospects of railway carriage building opened in Jurmala. Latek, who privatised the Riga Carriage Works, said it signed a co-operation deal with the Ukrainian coal-mining district of Donetsk, likely to become the plant's main customer.
- The heads of the securities committees of Latvia and Lithuania signed a letter of intent about creating a joint securities market in the Baltics. Estonia is likely to sign in September.
